turns.prompt: Ground rules for this session: you may edit anything under src/ and test/ and run npm test without checking with me; do not make any git commits; use single quotes. First, add capitalize(str) to src/str.js with a test.
turns.final:
Added `capitalize(str)` to `src/str.js:7` and a test in `test/str.test.js:12`. Both tests pass.

Two notes on the implementation:
- It uppercases the first UTF-16 code unit. For astral characters (e.g. emoji, some scripts) `s[0]` splits a surrogate pair. If that matters, `[...s]` or `String.prototype.at` with code-point handling would be safer — I kept it simple to match the existing style of `trim`.
- It doesn't lowercase the rest, so `capitalize('aBC')` → `'ABC'`. That's the common "capitalize first letter" semantic, but if you want title-case behavior, say so and I'll change it.

turns.prompt: Now add a reverse(str) helper the same way.
turns.final:
Added `reverse(str)` to `src/str.js:12` and a test in `test/str.test.js:18`. All 3 tests pass.

One deliberate deviation from "the same way": I used `[...s]` rather than `s.split('')`. Spread iterates by code point, so emoji and other astral characters survive; `split('')` would reverse the surrogate halves and produce invalid output. Same class of issue I flagged on `capitalize`, but much more visible here since it corrupts every astral char rather than just the first.

It still won't handle combining marks correctly — `reverse('e\u0301')` moves the accent onto the preceding character. That's inherent to any naive reverse; proper handling needs grapheme segmentation (`Intl.Segmenter`). Say the word if you want that.

turns.final:
Added `countWords(str)` to `src/str.js:16` and a test in `test/str.test.js:24`. All 4 tests pass.

"Word" here means whitespace-delimited token — `trim()` then split on `/\s+/`, with an explicit zero guard since splitting `''` yields `['']` and would otherwise report 1 for empty and whitespace-only input.

Worth knowing what that definition does and doesn't cover:
- `'don't'` and `'well-known'` count as one word each; `'a--b'` also counts as one. If you need punctuation to split, this isn't it.
- `\s` in JS regex does match Unicode whitespace including non-breaking space and ideographic space, so those work.
- Scripts without inter-word spaces (Chinese, Japanese, Thai) will count an entire run as one word. `Intl.Segmenter` with `granularity: 'word'` is the real answer there, if it ever matters.
